newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain mulls its options after clash with Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Spain mulls its options after clash with Cuba.

text.p: Spain accused Cuban leader Fidel Castro on Wednesday of manufacturing a diplomatic crisis with Madrid as a distraction from domestic troubles and said it did not rule out expelling the Cuban ambassador.
"All options are open," Foreign Minister Abel Matutes told a radio interviewer who asked him whether such an expulsion was possible.
Matutes later voiced concerns Cuba would sink into chaos if a transition to democracy was not completed before Castro goes.

"If this peaceful evolution is not achieved, when Castro disappears there will be upheavals, clashes, settling of scores and even spilling of blood, and that would not be a good scenario for Spanish business in Cuba," Matutes told reporters.

Months of rising tension between Cuba and Spain's young conservative government boiled over on Tuesday when Havana accused Madrid of meddling in its affairs and withdrew the approval it had already given for a new Spanish ambassador.
After 13 years of Socialist rule, Spain has now taken a tougher line against Castro and is nudging its European Union partners to press for democracy in Communist-ruled Cuba.
Matutes repeated on Wednesday his earlier assurances that Spain would not let itself be dragged into tit-for-tat escalation.
He accused Castro of trying to distract attention from the growing domestic problems of his country, which is under a United States trade embargo.
"It's typical of certain regimes, when they have internal difficulties, to invent a foreign enemy," Matutes said.
He reiterated Spain did not want Castro to retire but wanted him to implement a series of reforms himself.

Cuban ambassador Rosario Navas was called in to the foreign ministry in Madrid late on Tuesday to demand she assure special protection for the Spanish embassy in Havana after hundreds of local residents congregated around the mission, Matutes said.

In Havana, Cuban Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina and his deputy Isabel Allende met EU ambassadors on Tuesday -- except Spain's outgoing envoy Eudaldo Mirapeix -- to explain Cuba's decision against Mirapeix's appointed successor, Jose Coderch.

Allende later told reporters Cuba wanted to maintain relations with Spain. But she stressed that in Havana's view Madrid should adhere to principles of "mutual respect and non-interference" in its dealings with Havana.

Relations between Cuba and its former colonial power are at their lowest point since 1990. President Castro blasted Aznar without naming him in a speech on Sunday, accusing him of taking money from what he described as a mafia of Cuban exiles in Miami.
